newsitem.title: USA: US, Saudi energy officials discuss Iraq oil supply.
newsitem.headline: US, Saudi energy officials discuss Iraq oil supply.

text.p: Saudi and U.S. energy officials met Tuesday to discuss oil markets including Iraqi oil supplies and oil prices, according to associate deputy U.S. energy secretary Kyle Simpson.

In talks with Saudi oil minister Ali Naimi, U.S. energy officials talked about the impact of declining oil prices on the supply of Iraqi oil to the market under a United Nations agreement, which allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months.
Simpson told reporters that the Saudis had expressed no concerns about the spiraling effect of lower prices and increased supply.
"All we really talked about was how much oil is being supplied at this point and the effect on world markets," Simpson told reporters after the almost 2-1/2 hour meeting.
"They expressed what we've known all along - which is their desire to see a stable world market," he said.

Simpson said the officials had a "good candid discussion." Simpson said the most important thing that was reconfirmed in the meeting was "how important Saudi Arabia is as an oil supplier to the United States and to the world and the role they play as a reliable oil supplier."

Although U.S. officials said last week that they were going to discuss leasing out space in the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve to the Saudis, the issue did not come up at the meeting. He also said that there was no discussion of any oil-for-planes deal.

The U.S. and Saudi officials discussed their starkly differing views on policies to combat global warming. U.S. officials assured the Saudis that the Clinton administration had no plans to use a carbon tax to help curb burning of fossil fuels, which contributes to global warming.
"We mentioned we'd tried that and that didn't work," Simpson said referring to a proposal made four year ago to impose a BTU tax. "We don't see any plans anywhere about carbon taxes."

Simpson said it was understandable that the United States, the world'd largest oil consumer, and Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer, should have such different views on global warming policies.
In talking about oil price volatility, Simpson said U.S. officials pointed to oil company practices of keeping low inventories.

"We talked about what appears to be a new characteristic of world oil markets and that's price volatility at the margins and we have said that low inventory practices tend to contribute to that volatility," Simpson said.
U.S. and Saudi officials also discussed sharing information on oil price, supply and demand forecasts, Simpson said.
"We might see some steps we want to do on supply forecasts and demand," Simpson said.
